## 00_GettingStarted
- [notebooks/00_GettingStarted/01_environment_setup.ipynb](notebooks/00_GettingStarted/01_environment_setup.ipynb) — 01 — Environment Setup — Confirm your tools are installed and run your very first quantum circuit, so everything that follows runs cleanly.
- [notebooks/00_GettingStarted/02_what_is_optimal_transport.ipynb](notebooks/00_GettingStarted/02_what_is_optimal_transport.ipynb) — 02 — What Is Optimal Transport? — Build the central idea of the whole course by hand: moving a pile of mass into a new shape at the least possible cost.
## 01_QuantumFoundations
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/01_amplitudes_and_superposition.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/01_amplitudes_and_superposition.ipynb) — 01 — Amplitudes & Superposition — Write a qubit as a pair of complex amplitudes and meet superposition — the first idea with no classical-bit counterpart.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/02_why_amplitudes_are_complex.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/02_why_amplitudes_are_complex.ipynb) — 02 — Why Amplitudes Are Complex — Answer the question `01/01` set aside: why a qubit's amplitudes are *complex* numbers, and what the phase they carry actually does.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/03_the_bloch_sphere.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/03_the_bloch_sphere.ipynb) — 03 — The Bloch Sphere — Turn every pure qubit into a single point on a sphere — the compass we navigate by for the rest of the course.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/04_measurement_and_born_rule.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/04_measurement_and_born_rule.ipynb) — 04 — Measurement & the Born Rule — Turn amplitudes into the probabilities a measurement actually returns — and discover the one thing a measurement cannot see.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/05_inner_product_and_dirac.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/05_inner_product_and_dirac.ipynb) — 05 — The Inner Product & Dirac Notation — Learn the one piece of algebra every later notebook leans on: the inner product $\langle\varphi|\psi\rangle$ that turns two states into a single number.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/06_gates_as_unitary_evolution.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/06_gates_as_unitary_evolution.ipynb) — 06 — Gates as Unitary Evolution — Meet the operations that *move* a qubit, and discover why keeping every probability intact forces every one of them to be unitary.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/07_gates_as_bloch_rotations.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/07_gates_as_bloch_rotations.ipynb) — 07 — Gates as Rotations of the Bloch Sphere — See what unitarity buys: a gate is fixed only up to a global phase, it can always be undone, and on the Bloch sphere it is a rigid rotation, never a mirror image.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/08_pauli_gates.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/08_pauli_gates.ipynb) — 08 — The Pauli Gates — Meet $X$, $Y$, $Z$ — the three most important single-qubit gates — and their double life as both operations *and* observables.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/09_hadamard_and_measurement_bases.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/09_hadamard_and_measurement_bases.ipynb) — 09 — Hadamard & Measurement Bases — Meet the gate every circuit opens with, and turn it around to *measure in a different basis* — the recipe that explains the `h` and `sdg` you will see in `01/12` and `01/16`.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/10_phase_and_rotation_gates.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/10_phase_and_rotation_gates.ipynb) — 10 — Phase & Rotation Gates — Pick up the dials that send a qubit to *any* point on the Bloch sphere: the phase gates $S, S^\dagger, P(\lambda)$ and the continuous rotations $R_x, R_y, R_z$.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/11_expectation_values.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/11_expectation_values.ipynb) — 11 — Expectation Values — Make precise the single number a real experiment reports — the expectation value $\langle A\rangle = \langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle$ — as an *average of measurement outcomes*, size its error bar, and build the bridge to tomography.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/12_shot_noise_and_first_circuit.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/12_shot_noise_and_first_circuit.ipynb) — 12 — Shot Noise & Your First Circuit — Turn the one-qubit toolkit of `01/01`–`01/11` into something a quantum computer can *run*: write a circuit, let a simulated device execute it shot by shot, read the counts, and check that everything you derived — the Born shadow, the native gates, the error bar — shows up in the data. Then hear the first honest complaint of a real machine.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/13_from_states_to_density_matrix.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/13_from_states_to_density_matrix.ipynb) — 13 — From States to the Density Matrix — Promote a state vector to an operator — the density matrix $\rho = |\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ — build it by hand, read where each piece of information lives in it, redo everything you know (Born rule, expectation values, gates) in its language, and meet the central character of the rest of the course.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/14_pure_vs_mixed.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/14_pure_vs_mixed.ipynb) — 14 — Pure vs Mixed — Fill the slot: build statistical mixtures of states, meet the maximally mixed state $I/2$, set it beside $|+\rangle$ — same diagonal, no coherence — find the measurement that tells them apart, learn to measure "how mixed" with purity, and hold the single contrast the whole course is built to explain.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/15_fidelity_and_trace_distance.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/15_fidelity_and_trace_distance.ipynb) — 15 — Fidelity & Trace Distance — Turn the inside of the sphere into the **Bloch ball**, and pick up two honest yardsticks for "how different are two states?": the **trace distance**, which for a qubit is half the straight-line distance between Bloch vectors and tells you the best odds of telling two states apart in one shot, and the **fidelity**, which extends the inner product of `01/05` to mixed states — with its convention fixed once and for all for the rest of the course.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/16_tomography_of_a_noisy_qubit.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/16_tomography_of_a_noisy_qubit.ipynb) — 16 — Tomography of a Noisy Qubit — Close the density arc: run the three-axis recipe of `01/11` as the three circuits of `01/12` on a simulator that carries a real device's noise, rebuild $\rho$ from the counts, place it in the Bloch ball of `01/15`, read its purity, its fidelity to the state you meant to prepare and its trace distance from it — then be honest about *where* the shortfall comes from, and watch a genuinely mixed state appear when the qubit is left to idle.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/17_tensor_and_partial_trace.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/17_tensor_and_partial_trace.ipynb) — 17 — Tensor Product & Partial Trace — Put two qubits on one stage — the tensor product, written out entry by entry — then learn to ask what one of them is doing on its own: the **partial trace**, the quantum marginal, computed by hand on a $4\times4$ matrix before any helper is called. Along the way you meet the *third* way a state can be mixed: not a tossed coin (`01/14`), not decoherence (`01/16`), but being part of something larger.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/18_cnot_and_two_qubit_gates.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/18_cnot_and_two_qubit_gates.ipynb) — 18 — CNOT & Two-Qubit Gates — Meet the first gate that acts on two qubits *at once*: build CNOT by hand from its truth table as a $4\times4$ permutation matrix, check it is unitary, read it as a controlled-$X$, let it act on a superposition and watch a product state come out as a non-product — the Bell state, built from gates. Then run the same two gates as a Qiskit circuit and translate Qiskit's right-to-left qubit numbering into the convention of `01/17`.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/19_entanglement.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/19_entanglement.ipynb) — 19 — Entanglement — Give a name and a number to what CNOT manufactured in `01/18`: a two-qubit state that is perfectly definite as a whole yet whose parts are maximally uncertain. Define entanglement for pure states, measure it by the entropy of a part computed by hand, and then be careful — the same entropy on a *mixed* whole measures nothing: the correlated coins of `01/17` have one full bit of it and no entanglement at all. You will learn the test that works for mixtures too, and the second-basis measurement that tells a Bell pair from a shared coin.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/20_quantum_channels.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/20_quantum_channels.ipynb) — 20 — Quantum Channels — The last foundation: how a state changes when it is *not* alone. Derive the general quantum evolution — a **channel** — by hand from three things you already own (a unitary, a tensor product, a partial trace), read off its Kraus operators, and see why "decoherence" is entanglement with an environment you then trace out. Then find out what *completely* positive adds, meet the stochastic matrix as the channel that lives on the diagonal, and build the three standard qubit channels on the Bloch ball. Putting two of them on a clock is the work of `01/21`.
- [notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/21_t1_and_t2_channels.ipynb](notebooks/01_QuantumFoundations/21_t1_and_t2_channels.ipynb) — 21 — The $T_1$ and $T_2$ Channels of a Qubit from a Real Calibration — `01/20` derived the general evolution of an open qubit — a channel, written with Kraus operators — and built dephasing, amplitude damping and depolarizing, each at a fixed strength. What it left out is time. In `01/16` a qubit idled before readout, and its coherence fell as $e^{-t/T_2}$ while its $\langle Z\rangle$ rose toward $1$ (the qubit relaxing to $|0\rangle$) as $1 - e^{-t/T_1}$; today you put two of `01/20`'s channels on a clock and find that those two laws are exactly what they become. The $T_1$ and $T_2$ are those of a stored calibration snapshot of a real device, and the idle is simulated from them.
## 02_InformationAndGeometry
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/01_shannon_entropy.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/01_shannon_entropy.ipynb) — 01 — Shannon Entropy — Measure uncertainty as average surprise — the first tool of information theory and the spine of everything that follows. Build the formula from the one property surprise must have, compute it by hand before calling any helper, prove the two facts every later notebook leans on (the uniform distribution is the most uncertain; a part is never more uncertain than the whole, $H(A) \le H(AB)$), and see why that second fact is exactly what the Bell state of `01/19` breaks.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/02_kl_divergence.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/02_kl_divergence.ipynb) — 02 — KL Divergence — Measure the cost of a wrong model: the *extra bits* you pay for coding with $q$ when the truth is $p$. You will build the formula from the mismatched code of `02/01`, prove by hand that this cost is never negative (Gibbs' inequality), and collect what that one fact buys: the uniform law is the most uncertain one, and no prefix code beats the entropy. Then you will meet the three ways relative entropy is *not* a distance: it is asymmetric, infinite off the support, and without a triangle inequality. What it obeys in place of the distance axioms is the subject of `02/03`.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/03_laws_of_relative_entropy.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/03_laws_of_relative_entropy.ipynb) — 03 — The Laws of Relative Entropy — `02/02` built the relative entropy $D(p\|q) = \sum_x p_x\log_2\frac{p_x}{q_x}$ as the extra bits per symbol of coding with a model $q$ when the truth is $p$, proved that it is never negative (Gibbs' inequality), and showed the three ways it fails to be a distance. What it left open is why the course builds on it anyway. Today's answer is three laws that make it the currency of information. It adds up over independent symbols, which no bounded distance can do. It is jointly convex, and strictly so in its first argument, which total variation is not. And it never grows under processing, a law it shares with total variation (you proved the trace-distance version in `01/20`, exercise 4). One inequality proves the last two.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/04_mutual_information.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/04_mutual_information.ipynb) — 04 — Mutual Information — Measure how much two variables share — the bits one carries about the other. Build it as the relative entropy of `02/02` pointed at a joint table and its own product of marginals, compute it by hand on the three tables of `02/01` §3, derive its three faces ($D$ of the joint, a difference of entropies, a saved conditional entropy), prove the ceiling that two bits can never share more than one bit (the ceiling a Bell pair will clear in `02/11`), meet the conditional version and the data-processing inequality that `02/05` is built on, and learn why a mutual information *estimated from data* is biased upward — the first honesty check of every coupling analysis.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/05_transfer_entropy.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/05_transfer_entropy.ipynb) — 05 — Transfer Entropy — Close the classical-information arc: make information flow **directed** — who drives whom — by naming the axes of `02/04`'s conditional mutual information by time, compute it by hand on a system whose true table you can write down, see exactly why the conditioning matters (lagged mutual information reports a backward flow that does not exist; transfer entropy does not), and then earn the honesty rules every estimate from signals needs: the plug-in bias, the surrogate that preserves autocorrelation, the lag, the history length, and the synergy that no pairwise measure can see. This is the measure most used to probe directed coupling in interacting systems — the kind of question hyperscanning asks of two brains — and it is the last classical stone before the quantum lifts.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/06_the_probability_simplex.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/06_the_probability_simplex.ipynb) — 06 — The Probability Simplex — See the space of *all* categorical distributions as one geometric object — a triangle for three outcomes — and learn its anatomy by hand: where the certain outcomes sit, where the uniform sits, what an edge means, why a mixture never leaves it, how a distribution *is* its own barycentric coordinates. Then draw on it the quantities of `02/01`–`02/04` — entropy as a hill, relative entropy as an asymmetric bowl, the independence surface that mutual information measures the distance to — and finally ask the question that opens the geometry arc: **how far apart are two points of this triangle?** You already own four candidate answers, and they disagree. Deciding between them is `02/07`–`02/09`.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/07_fisher_rao_metric.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/07_fisher_rao_metric.ipynb) — 07 — The Fisher–Rao Metric — Answer the question `02/06` left open — which ruler is natural on the simplex? — with a criterion, not a preference: two distributions are close when *samples cannot tell them apart*. Make that precise by hand for a coin (the length of a step is the number of standard errors it moves the sample mean), derive the Fisher information $I(\theta) = 1/\theta(1-\theta)$ twice — from the score, and as the Hessian of relative entropy — and see it diverge at the boundary: every step near a corner is expensive (the corners themselves stay at a finite distance — `02/08` computes it — because the blow-up is only like $1/\sqrt p$). Extend it to three outcomes, $ds^2 = \sum_i dp_i^2/p_i$, draw the *unit circles* of this metric across the triangle and watch them squeeze against the edges, and finally meet the theorem that makes it *the* choice: Chentsov's — the only metric that does not change when you split an outcome into sub-outcomes and never grows when you merge outcomes. The geodesics and the closed-form distance are `02/08`'s.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/08_fisher_rao_geodesics.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/08_fisher_rao_geodesics.ipynb) — 08 — Fisher–Rao Geodesics — `02/07` left you with a curved triangle: a metric $ds^2 = \sum_i dp_i^2/p_i$ that charges $1/p_i$ for moving outcome $i$, so that steps near the boundary are expensive. This notebook turns that metric into lengths of whole paths, finds the shortest ones, and measures them. The key is one change of variable, $\phi_i = \sqrt{p_i}$, which turns the curved triangle into a piece of a sphere. From there follow the closed-form distance $d_{FR}(p, q) = 2\arccos\big(\sum_i\sqrt{p_i q_i}\big)$, the finite distance to a corner, and a new reading of the Bhattacharyya overlap and the Hellinger distance. You finish by computing a geodesic by hand and measuring how far it bulges.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/09_two_geometries_one_simplex.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/09_two_geometries_one_simplex.ipynb) — 09 — Two Geometries on One Simplex — Close the geometry arc with the punchline that powers the rest of the course: the same simplex carries *two* distinct geometries — information and transport — and they give different answers to "what is the halfway distribution?"
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/10_umegaki_relative_entropy.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/10_umegaki_relative_entropy.ipynb) — 10 — Umegaki Relative Entropy — Lift the relative entropy of `02/02` to density matrices. You will compute the **Umegaki relative entropy** $S(\rho\|\sigma) = \mathrm{tr}\,\rho\,(\log_2\rho - \log_2\sigma)$ by hand, watch it give one bit for $|+\rangle$ against $I/2$, whose $Z$ statistics are identical, and check the three properties `02/02` and `02/03` asked of a quantum lift: never negative (Klein), infinite exactly when the support of $\rho$ is not contained in that of $\sigma$, and never increased by a channel (Lindblad).
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/11_quantum_mutual_information.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/11_quantum_mutual_information.ipynb) — 11 — Quantum Mutual Information — Lift mutual information to density matrices, and meet the first quantity of the course that reads correlation of every kind at once. You will compute $I(A{:}B) = S(A) + S(B) - S(AB)$ by hand from the eigenvalues of three $4\times4$ matrices. The correlated coins of `01/17` and the Bell pair of `01/18` come back side by side, as `01/21` announced, and part company: the coins share $1$ bit, exactly the classical ceiling of `02/04`, and the Bell pair shares $2$ bits. You will learn what that excess certifies (entanglement) and what it does not make of $I$ (an entanglement meter). Finally you will prove the property `02/04` promised: no channel applied to one side alone can increase $I(A{:}B)$.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/12_negative_conditional_entropy.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/12_negative_conditional_entropy.ipynb) — 12 — Negative Conditional Entropy — Meet the sharpest signature of entanglement: a conditional entropy that drops below zero — impossible for any classical pair.
- [notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/13_bures_distance.ipynb](notebooks/02_InformationAndGeometry/13_bures_distance.ipynb) — 13 — Bures Distance — Close Module 02: lift the Fisher–Rao distance to density matrices, and complete the classical-to-quantum information dictionary.
## 03_ClassicalOptimalTransport
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/01_the_monge_problem.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/01_the_monge_problem.ipynb) — 01 — The Monge Problem — Ask optimal transport's founding question — *what is the cheapest way to reshape one pile of mass into another?* — and meet Monge's original answer: a deterministic map.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/02_where_monge_breaks.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/02_where_monge_breaks.ipynb) — 02 — Where Monge Breaks — Meet the obstruction that defeats Monge's deterministic map: when one pile of mass must *split* to fill another, no function can describe the move.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/03_the_kantorovich_lp.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/03_the_kantorovich_lp.ipynb) — 03 — The Kantorovich LP — Relax Monge's map into a *coupling* that may split mass, and optimal transport becomes a linear program that always has a solution.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/04_birkhoff_and_assignment.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/04_birkhoff_and_assignment.ipynb) — 04 — Birkhoff and the Assignment Problem — Close the Monge→Kantorovich arc with its most elegant special case — uniform marginals, where transport becomes the classical assignment problem — and open the transport row of the classical↔quantum dictionary.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/05_wasserstein_distance.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/05_wasserstein_distance.ipynb) — 05 — The Wasserstein Distance — Promote the Kantorovich *cost* into a genuine *distance* — one that, unlike the KL divergence, listens to the geometry of the ground space.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/06_1d_quantile_closed_form.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/06_1d_quantile_closed_form.ipynb) — 06 — The 1-D Closed Form — On the line, the whole linear program collapses to *sort and match by quantile* — and $W_1$ becomes the plain area between two cumulative curves.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/07_mccann_geodesic.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/07_mccann_geodesic.ipynb) — 07 — The McCann Geodesic — Close the Wasserstein arc with its most beautiful feature: the $W_2$ geodesic *slides* mass through the ground space — the transport-geometry half of the two-geometries hinge.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/08_kantorovich_duality.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/08_kantorovich_duality.ipynb) — 08 — Kantorovich Duality — Every transport LP has a hidden twin: a *dual* that prices positions instead of moving mass. The two views give the same number — and the dual is where the deep structure lives.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/09_entropic_regularization.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/09_entropic_regularization.ipynb) — 09 — Entropic Regularization — Reward the transport plan a little for being *spread out*, and the problem turns smooth, strongly convex, and fast. At its heart sits one object: the Gibbs kernel.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/10_sinkhorn_algorithm.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/10_sinkhorn_algorithm.ipynb) — 10 — The Sinkhorn Algorithm — Bend the Gibbs kernel onto the marginal constraints by nothing more than rescaling rows and columns in turn. Five lines, two matrix products per step — the algorithm that made optimal transport fast.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/11_amari_bridge.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/11_amari_bridge.ipynb) — 11 — Amari's Bridge — The identity the whole course has been walking toward: the Sinkhorn plan is the **KL projection** of the Gibbs kernel onto the transportation polytope. Transport geometry *is* information geometry. The name *Amari's bridge* is the course's own label, chosen because the identity lands in the information geometry Amari developed; the identity itself is the reading of entropic transport as a Kullback–Leibler projection, due to Cuturi (2013) and Benamou et al. (2015).
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/12_bures_wasserstein.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/12_bures_wasserstein.ipynb) — 12 — Bures–Wasserstein — For one special family — the Gaussians — optimal transport needs no algorithm at all. $W_2$ is a closed-form expression in the means and covariances.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/13_the_bures_bridge.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/13_the_bures_bridge.ipynb) — 13 — The Bures Bridge — Watch one formula change identity. The matrix term of the Gaussian Wasserstein distance, fed density matrices instead of covariances, *becomes* the quantum Bures distance of `02/13`. This is the door into quantum optimal transport.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/14_gaussian_geodesic.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/14_gaussian_geodesic.ipynb) — 14 — The Gaussian Geodesic — Follow the shortest path between two Gaussians and see that it never leaves the Gaussian family: every point of the path is a Gaussian, whose mean slides along a line and whose covariance ellipse turns and rescales. This is the place where the optimal path between continuous distributions in the plane, and not only the distance, can be written down in full.
- [notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/15_benamou_brenier_otto.ipynb](notebooks/03_ClassicalOptimalTransport/15_benamou_brenier_otto.ipynb) — 15 — Benamou–Brenier and Otto — Watch the Wasserstein geodesic as a *flow* whose kinetic energy is exactly the squared distance $W_2^2$, and read what that says about the shape of the space of distributions.
## 04_QuantumOptimalTransport
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/01_diagonal_collapse.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/01_diagonal_collapse.ipynb) — 01 — The Diagonal-Collapse Problem — Open quantum optimal transport with the question that makes it necessary: *if we reduce a quantum state to the probabilities a measurement returns, what do we throw away?*
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/02_noncommuting_same_diagonal.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/02_noncommuting_same_diagonal.ipynb) — 02 — Non-Commuting States, Same Diagonal — In `01_diagonal_collapse` you saw two *different* states share a $Z$-diagonal; here you meet a sharper version of the same trap — two states that do not even commute, yet still collapse onto the identical diagonal.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/03_trevisan_taxonomy.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/03_trevisan_taxonomy.ipynb) — 03 — Trevisan's Taxonomy and the Consistency Principle — Synthesise the opening arc of Module 4: turn the two examples you built into a *law* every quantum optimal transport must obey, then place the competing definitions of QOT on one map.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/04_quantum_coupling_sdp.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/04_quantum_coupling_sdp.ipynb) — 04 — The Quantum Coupling SDP — Build the object the taxonomy named: a *quantum coupling* of two states, optimised by a semidefinite program — the operator-level lift of the Kantorovich LP.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/05_solving_qot_in_cvxpy.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/05_solving_qot_in_cvxpy.ipynb) — 05 — Solving Quantum OT in cvxpy — Point the coupling SDP at the example the module has carried since the start — separate $|+\rangle\langle+|$ from $I/2$, read the optimal coupling, and add to the dictionary the three rows this arc earns.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/06_entropic_qot_gibbs.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/06_entropic_qot_gibbs.ipynb) — 06 — Entropic Quantum OT and the Gibbs Kernel — Smooth the coupling SDP the way module 03 smoothed the Kantorovich LP — add a von Neumann entropy bonus $-\varepsilon\,S(\rho_{AB})$ — and watch the **matrix-exponential Gibbs kernel** $K = \exp(-C/\varepsilon)$ appear at the centre of the regularised problem.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/07_operator_sinkhorn_iteration.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/07_operator_sinkhorn_iteration.ipynb) — 07 — The Operator Sinkhorn Iteration — In `04/06` a black-box convex solver handed us the entropic quantum optimal-transport plan. Here we build the explicit **operator Sinkhorn iteration** that *reaches* that same optimum on its own when the states and the cost commute — alternating positive-operator rescalings of the Gibbs kernel, the matrix lift of the row/column rescaling that made classical transport fast in `03/10`.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/08_quantum_amari_bridge.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/08_quantum_amari_bridge.ipynb) — 08 — The Quantum Amari Bridge — The single identity the whole quantum arc has been walking toward: the entropic quantum optimal-transport plan is the **Umegaki relative-entropy projection** of the matrix-exponential Gibbs kernel $K = \exp(-C/\varepsilon)$ onto the set of couplings. The operator lift of `03/11`'s classical Amari identity — transport geometry *is* information geometry, now for density matrices. (*Amari's bridge* is the course's own name for that identity, as `03/11` explains; you will not find it under that name in the literature.)
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/09_the_qot_zoo.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/09_the_qot_zoo.ipynb) — 09 — The QOT Zoo — Put all three quantum optimal-transport objects on one bench and ask the question the module has been circling: when do they give the *same* number, and when do they part ways? The honest answer is the whole point — they are a **reconciled family**, agreeing exactly in some regimes, ordered identically in others, and genuinely distinct in the rest.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/10_embedding_signals_into_states.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/10_embedding_signals_into_states.ipynb) — 10 — Embedding signals into states — To *do* quantum optimal transport on a signal, you first face a modelling choice that decides everything downstream: **how does a signal become a quantum state?** This notebook lays out the embedding menu, writes each state by hand, builds the one object the capstone feeds to every quantum measure (the time-averaged joint state of two signals), and names exactly what each step keeps and what it throws away.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/11_moments_the_joint_state_reads.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/11_moments_the_joint_state_reads.ipynb) — 11 — The moments a joint state reads — `04/10` turned signals into states: three per-sample embeddings, a covariance density for a whole record, and the time-averaged joint state $\rho_{AB}$ of two signals, whose every entry is the time average of one phase factor. It left two bright entries in the joint state of a locked pair without saying what they hold. This notebook reads them. You will find which **circular moments of the phase difference** each embedding's joint state carries, and see on a small toy what an embedding that carries one more moment can tell apart.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/12_kuramoto_dyad_and_ground_truth.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/12_kuramoto_dyad_and_ground_truth.ipynb) — 12 — The Kuramoto dyad and the ground truth — The capstone begins here. Before we can ask whether a *quantum* coupling measure earns its keep, we need a problem where we already know the answer — a synthetic system whose coupling we *injected ourselves*, so "does the measure follow it?" becomes a question with a checkable answer. This notebook builds that test bed: two coupled **Kuramoto oscillators** with a known coupling strength $K$, and the two **classical baselines** every later measure is set beside.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/13_naive_phase_embedding_tracks_K.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/13_naive_phase_embedding_tracks_K.ipynb) — 13 — The naive phase embedding tracks $K$ — You hold a test bed with a known answer and two classical yardsticks. Now we make the first move of the capstone proper: carry the dyad's phases across the bridge from `04/10`, turn each phase into a **quantum state**, and ask the question the whole module is building toward — does a *quantum* coupling measure read the injected coupling $K$ as faithfully as PLV does?
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/14_the_redundancy_reveal.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/14_the_redundancy_reveal.ipynb) — 14 — The redundancy reveal — Notebook `04/13` ended on a win and a question. The quantum measures rose with the injected coupling $K$ exactly as the classical baselines did — *it looked like it works*. But "rises with $K$" is the bar `04/12` set, and PLV already clears it. So here we ask the sharper question head-on: **does the quantum measure read anything PLV does not?** The answer we find is a real, clean result — and it points us straight at the fix.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/15_richer_embedding_applied.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/15_richer_embedding_applied.ipynb) — 15 — The richer embedding, applied — Notebook `04/14` left us with a sharp, structural diagnosis: on the **naive phase qubit**, the joint state $\rho_{AB}$ has a single coupling-dependent number in it, and that number is the phase-locking value. Feed a quantum measure a state that only knows PLV and it can only report PLV. The bottleneck was never quantum optimal transport — it was the embedding. This notebook builds the fix.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/16_discriminating_experiment.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/16_discriminating_experiment.ipynb) — 16 — The discriminating experiment — This is the experiment the capstone has been preparing. In `04/15` you opened a second channel in the joint state $\rho_{AB}$ — the second circular moment of the phase difference, a quantity the phase-locking value cannot see. Today you put that channel to a controlled test: you build two systems that PLV is unable to tell apart, you watch a richer quantum coupling measure separate them, and then you do what a careful experimenter does next — you set a classical statistic of the same second moment beside it and score every measure with one protocol.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/17_capstone_synthesis.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/17_capstone_synthesis.ipynb) — 17 — The capstone synthesis — In `04/16` you scored a quantum measure and its classical neighbour on ensembles drawn by hand, and you left with two limits: one pair of ensembles, and a second moment you turned yourself. Today you lift both. You meet a pair of coupled oscillators whose second harmonic moves on its own, you read what a **bench** measured on it — one model and one protocol, run once, with its results committed — and you write the accounting of the capstone from those measurements.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/18_embedding_design_amplifies_the_effect.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/18_embedding_design_amplifies_the_effect.ipynb) — 18 — Embedding design amplifies the effect — In `04/17` the equal-weight qutrit read the second harmonic, and needed longer records than the second-harmonic PLV to do it. This notebook turns a dial the capstone left at its default, the **weights** of the harmonics. You will first find on paper where each harmonic sits in the joint density and how a weight moves it. Then you will measure what it buys, and see why the gain stops where the matching classical statistic already stands. A lever of another kind, the amplitude embedding, is the subject of `04/19`.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/19_amplitude_embedding_and_phase_amplitude_coupling.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/19_amplitude_embedding_and_phase_amplitude_coupling.ipynb) — 19 — The amplitude embedding and phase–amplitude coupling — In `04/18` you turned the weights of the harmonics of the qutrit embedding: the quantum measure came to need about as few samples as the second-harmonic PLV, and with the first harmonic switched off it became that classical statistic on another scale. Every embedding there wrote phases only. What is still missing is a coupling that lives in the *amplitude* of a signal, which no phase statistic can see; this notebook scores the embedding that reaches it, beside the classical statistic built for the job.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/20_what_no_classical_data_embedding_can_buy.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/20_what_no_classical_data_embedding_can_buy.ipynb) — 20 — What no classical-data embedding can buy — In `04/18` and `04/19` neither lever took the quantum measure past the matching classical statistic: the weights brought it level with the second-harmonic PLV, and the amplitude embedding was behind on short records and at the ceiling with it from 2,000 samples on. Now we ask the sharpest question of the whole capstone: is there *any* embedding — even one that **entangles** the two systems — that lets a quantum-optimal-transport measure detect coupling structure **no** classical statistic can? The answer is **no**, and it is a proposition you can prove in a few lines; an experiment then illustrates it, entangling gate included. Seeing *why* turns the capstone's caveat into a precise structural boundary, and tells us exactly where a genuinely quantum advantage *would* have to come from.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/21_vqe_limitation_de_palma.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/21_vqe_limitation_de_palma.ipynb) — 21 — The De Palma limitation: when quantum optimal transport bounds the algorithm — Turn the geometry around. Across this module you used quantum optimal transport to *measure* — to read the coupling between two systems off a density matrix. Here you meet a result where quantum optimal transport becomes a *proof technique*: transport inequalities, built on Wasserstein distances of order 1, limit what shallow variational quantum algorithms can achieve, drawing a provable line around a whole family of near-term quantum methods.
- [notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/22_frontier_synthesis.ipynb](notebooks/04_QuantumOptimalTransport/22_frontier_synthesis.ipynb) — 22 — Frontier and synthesis: the theory in one frame — The last notebook of Module 04, and the close of the theory. Bring the journey so far back into a single view — Modules 00 to 04 in one line each, twenty canonical numerical results of Modules 02 to 04 replayed live, what the capstone measured, stated with its limits, and the classical ↔ quantum dictionary read in its completed form. This is a celebration with the receipts laid out beside it. One module remains after this one: in Module 05 you run what you built on a real quantum processor, and the course ends there.
## 05_RealQuantumHardware
- [notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/01_using_a_real_quantum_computer.ipynb](notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/01_using_a_real_quantum_computer.ipynb) — 01 — Using a Real Quantum Computer — This notebook hands you the keys to an actual IBM quantum processor: you take a quantity you have so far computed *exactly* on the simulator and re-run it, unchanged, on real hardware.
- [notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/02_born_rule_on_real_hardware.ipynb](notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/02_born_rule_on_real_hardware.ipynb) — 02 — The Born Rule on Real Hardware — In `01/04` you sampled the Born rule on a simulator; now you read it straight off a real QPU and look for the device's read-out bias.
- [notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/03_tomography_and_fidelity_on_real_hardware.ipynb](notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/03_tomography_and_fidelity_on_real_hardware.ipynb) — 03 — Tomography & Fidelity on Real Hardware — Counts hand you probabilities — one number per outcome. But the device prepared a *whole* state, with phases and coherences that a single histogram cannot see. To recover all of it you measure in three complementary bases and reconstruct the state, then ask the honest question: how far did it fall from the ideal you asked for?
- [notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/04_quantum_mutual_information_on_real_hardware.ipynb](notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/04_quantum_mutual_information_on_real_hardware.ipynb) — 04 — Quantum Mutual Information on Real Hardware — In `02/11` a Bell pair shared exactly 2 bits of mutual information — double the classical maximum any pair of bits can reach. That factor of two *is* entanglement, written in the language of information. Here you measure that same quantity on a real superconducting chip and watch decoherence quietly steal a piece of it.
- [notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/05_geometry_on_real_hardware_bures.ipynb](notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/05_geometry_on_real_hardware_bures.ipynb) — 05 — Geometry on Real Hardware: the Bures Distance — How far did the device's state fall from the ideal you asked for? In `05/03` you answered with a fidelity below 1 — an honest score, but a *number*, not yet a *distance*. Here you turn it into one. The gap becomes a single point on the Bures geometry you built in `02/13`, and then you add circuit depth and test whether that point moves outward. On the offline model of the device it does, step by step; on the real device, one pass per depth could not resolve the rise.
- [notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/06_capstone_on_real_hardware_and_frontier.ipynb](notebooks/05_RealQuantumHardware/06_capstone_on_real_hardware_and_frontier.ipynb) — 06 — The Capstone on Real Hardware, and the Frontier — In Module 04 you asked whether a quantum coupling measure reads something the phase-locking value (PLV) cannot, and you wrote down what the measurements showed. With an embedding that carries the second harmonic it reads past PLV. A classical statistic of the same two harmonics reads as far, from shorter records. What quantum optimal transport brings is one common geometry. Every number in that accounting was computed on a classical computer, from density matrices written out exactly. Here we ask the hardware question that closes the course. The two ensembles of `04/16` have different quantum mutual informations (QMI), and we call that difference a **gap**. It is **0.0044 nat** with the equal-weight embedding of `04/16`, and **0.0145 nat** once the first harmonic is turned down to a weight of 0.2, as in `04/18`. Is a real quantum processor sharp enough to resolve gaps that small? We will answer with numbers, and the answer will show where the frontier lies.
## Course-wide
- [notebooks/dictionary.ipynb](notebooks/dictionary.ipynb) — The classical ↔ quantum dictionary — This is the one table that gathers what the course translates between the classical world and the quantum one. Each row reads from left to right: a classical object on the left, and the quantum object that plays its part on the right. Some rows are translations, some are contrasts, and a contrast is as much a result as a match.
